title: Once-More: Continuous Self-Correction for Large Language Models via Perplexity-Guided Intervention
one_liner: Intervene during generation at doubtful next-word choices so the model corrects itself before small mistakes snowball into a bad answer.
lead: Long generation often fails because a small early mistake pushes later words in the wrong direction, and the error compounds before any correction arrives. Once-More intervenes during generation instead of waiting until a full draft exists. It watches for doubtful next-word decisions, mixes in feedback from verifiers, and redistributes the next-word scores before the mistake is emitted. This helps because correction happens at the moment the path can still be changed cheaply.

problem.h2: Early generation mistakes can compound long before a final draft is reviewed
paras: A language model produces text one next word at a time. If it chooses a weak next word early, later choices are conditioned on that mistake, so the answer can drift, repeat itself, or reason from a false premise.

Many self-correction methods wait until a substantial draft has already been written. By then, the answer may be far from the right path, and a later revision has to repair a large amount of bad text. That is wasteful because the cheapest time to fix a wrong turn is before it becomes the base for many later steps.

callout.html: Detect doubtful next-word choices while generation is still in progress and steer them immediately using verifier feedback, because early course correction prevents later drift.

steps.text: At each step, compute the model's score spread over possible next words.
Check whether the current next-word choice looks doubtful under the model's own score spread.
Use external feedback signals to judge whether the current path looks promising.
Shift probability mass toward words that better match the verifier feedback, because that makes the chosen next word follow the stronger branch.

steps.b: Continue generation on the corrected path
steps.text: Emit the adjusted next word and repeat at the following step.

paras: The paper changes when and how self-correction happens. Instead of correcting a finished or half-finished draft, it modifies the next-word decision itself while text is being produced.

hidden.name: how resistant the generation path is to early drift
paras: The hidden quantity is trajectory stability: once the answer starts, how likely is it to stay on a correct path instead of drifting after one weak choice? A model with poor trajectory stability can look fine at the first few steps but fail badly later because every new word inherits earlier mistakes.

Once-More improves trajectory stability by acting at uncertain steps. That matters because uncertain steps are exactly where one bad choice can redirect the whole answer, so steering them early has outsized impact on the final result.

heat.caption: Darker cells mark the moments where intervention changes the whole later trajectory.

reads.html: The best moment to correct a long answer is the step where the model is uncertain and the path can still be redirected.
Continuous intervention improves self-correction because verifier-guided steering acts before local mistakes accumulate into global failure.

paras: Text generation is path dependent. Every next word becomes part of the context for later words, so an early mistake can trigger a cascade of later mistakes. A late-stage corrector has to undo many downstream consequences at once.

Once-More works earlier. It watches the model's next-word uncertainty and uses verifier feedback to reshape the score spread before the next word is chosen. This is effective because it changes the branch point itself, not just the later symptoms of a bad branch.

The intervention is continuous rather than one-shot. That matters because long answers may have several dangerous branch points, not just one. Repeated small corrections can keep the answer on a good trajectory with lower cost than throwing away a long bad draft and starting over, because each correction happens before later text has to be regenerated.

math.words: Take the model's original next-word scores and add a correction term from verifier feedback, then normalize the result into a new probability distribution.
math.equation: p_new(w) proportional to p_base(w) * exp(alpha * feedback(w))
symbols: the model's original probability for word w
the verifier's score for how good word w looks on the current path
how strongly verifier feedback changes the next-word choice
the corrected next-word probability after intervention

worked.title: A tiny worked example
lines: Suppose the model gives three candidate next words: A at 0.50, B at 0.30, and C at 0.20.
The verifier thinks B fits the reasoning path best, so feedback(A) = 0, feedback(B) = 1, feedback(C) = -1.
Adjusted unnormalized scores become 0.50 * exp(0), 0.30 * exp(1), and 0.20 * exp(-1), which are about 0.50, 0.82, and 0.07.
After normalization, B becomes the top next-word choice, so the answer follows the stronger path before a mistake is emitted.

math.note: The correction term does not rewrite the whole answer; it nudges the next branch point toward better continuations because the next-word choice is where the path can still change cheaply.

items.b: Bad verifier feedback can steer the model the wrong way.
items.html: If the verifier misjudges a branch point, the system may reinforce the wrong next word and push the answer farther from the truth.

items.b: Intervening too often can overconstrain generation.
items.html: If every mildly uncertain step triggers a strong correction, the answer may become rigid or repetitive because the natural flexibility of generation is suppressed.

items.b: Cheap uncertainty signals can miss subtle errors.
items.html: Some wrong paths look confident locally, so uncertainty alone may not flag them and they can slip through without intervention.
When uncertainty detection and verifier feedback are well calibrated, continuous intervention helps because it corrects weak branch points before they expand into long wrong trajectories.

demo.h2: What a runnable demo should prove
paras: Build a long-form reasoning or summarization system with three settings: no correction, late draft refinement, and continuous intervention. At each generation step, log the model's uncertainty, whether an intervention happened, and whether the final answer stayed correct. Compare final accuracy and the number of long drift failures.
demo.metric_eq: drift_reduction = long-drift failures without intervention - long-drift failures with continuous intervention
demo.closing: The demo should show that intervening at doubtful next-word choices reduces compounding errors because the generation path is corrected before weak local decisions harden into a bad full answer.
